questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I've always wanted to travel NZ, and especially to go there and stay for a longer period of time. So I thought exchange was the perfect opportunity to visit this beautiful country, get to know nice people doing the same thing, and to experience a different university and academic style etc. I chose Dunedin specifically because I'm from a big city, Copenhagen (and I study here as well), so I wanted to try a smaller, student city - which Dunedin is. Dunedin is close to wildlife and nature, is on the South Island (which I personally really wanted to travel), and has a great university campus and resources for students. This checked all my boxes: nature, good campus vibes, South Island.
Christchurch, Wellington and Auckland just seemed like too large cities to go study abroad in, because I chose NZ for the nature - but if you want a big city experience in NZ, I bet they are great.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: What a wonderful experience. This study abroad felt like a break from the usual routine at home, still studying but in a completely different setting, you're on your own and can do exactly what you please. Dunedin was a great place to come and just feel at home, kiwis are so friendly and welcoming, the University of Otago is great. I met really cool and friendly people (even friends for life), travelled a whoooole lot, and learned a lot about myself. NZ is just a stunning country.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Easy. The orientation week was very informative and had lots of events as well, so there is no lack of information upon arrival. They are really sweet as well.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I got my keys at the UniFlats office and the Campus Watch even drovev me home (I arrived at midnight).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I lived right next to campus, literally like 50 metres, so I basically did live on campus. It was easy to find the housing cause I got it through UniFlats, a university organized housing option for exchange students.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
It's nice to live close to campus, basically in the North Dunedin suburb. Campus is large, but everything is pretty close. 

Castle St and Hyde St are party streets (basically on campus as well).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I got literally the best, biggest house offered by UniFlats. Lived with 4 other women in a spacious house with a lovely rose garden right next to campus, and not on the party streets. 
The only thing with Dunedin housing, I think in all of NZ, is they don't know how to insulate their buildings. It gets cooooold, and all you get to heat your room is an electric heater which is very small. Can highly recommend getting a hot water bottle and thermals (wool). Also, a lot of the houses, as far as I understand, have mold. I developed a cough shortly after moving in which persisted almost my whole stay, it only let up when I travelled elsewhere. So that sucked, but there isn't really anything you can do about it. Still, my house was AWESOME.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You browse the courses, register them of their student portal eVision, and wait for approval. Then you accept their offer. (I think, it's a long time since I applied).

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Lots, there are emails to write to and they are super helpful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very succesful. I even changed courses which was easy enough, just had to get a new pre-approval from UCPH.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try something different, you have the chance with basically no risk cause it's just pass/fail for UCPH (at least is was for me). Browse the courses, find something you like and go for it!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
COMP161 was pretty high level for a first semester course - but I'm also a humanities student, so I probably found it more difficult than others would. 
MAOR102 was a nice level, pretty easy and interesting. 
ENGL220 was also not so overwhelming in the course load, also because English is my major so a lot of the material was repetition of my third semester anyways.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Really different in the way they assess your work. You do work throughout the semester which counts for x amount of your total grade - so this was really nice compared to the 100% of your grade being assessed at one exam, end of semester. The teaching style was pretty similar with lectures and classes, but you're mixed with people from all sorts of majors, not just your own major, so that was  different.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
MAOR102 - Maori Society 
ENGL220 - Creative Writing: Reading for Writers
COMP161 - Computer Programming

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
MAOR102 is great for exchange students, a loooot of people I knew took it. The Maori are New Zealand's indegenious peoples, and MAOR102 is a great first semester course introduction to Maori society, culture, history, colonization, and present social issues. It's a great way to learn and understand contemporary NZ political issues, its culture and history, etc. The course was easy to follow, 2 lectures a week and a weekly 1 hr tutorial. The workload wasn't too bad at all, but the exam was a bit specific with some of the details from the course, but it was fine. 

COMP161 was challenging for me because I study English and have no computer programming experience. They teach Java, and it is a lot of work. But I did learn a lot, and I passed the course - I expect it to be a bit easier if you have some programming experience or interest, just know you do need to put in some work to pass, but it's doable - I did it and I'm in the humanities.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
I don't know how much I spent on food, I often went out to eat (which isn't that cheap) but groceries are also expensive. 
Also don't know how much personal spending I did, A LOT is the answer. I traveled a lot and did a bunch of activities that were not cheap - but worth it!

Communication (phone number and data) is more expensive than in DK. A good tip is to buy a package duty free in the airport when you land, I got Spark for 2x3 months with unlimited data and that was great. it was around 1000 kr. for 6 months use (ish) and that's apparently really good price.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Some things in the supermarket are really expensive (like 25 kr. for 1 avocado) because they have to be imported I guess - it really is island life. 

Coffee 'only' cost like 30 ish kr. for a large latte, so that was less expensive than I expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The tramping club offers a lot of events and trips, that was great. If you're a member you can also rent tramping gear for free (sleeping bags, sleeping mats, trangia etc). 
The OUCC (canoe club) was also great, they offer white-water kayak trips. I joined one because I have prior kayaking experience, but this was like nothing I've ever experienced before. The kayaking was terrifying for me, so I only went once, but the vibes on the trip was amazing. I can highly recommend if you're into adventure and trying something new!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
UniPol is a free gym with lots of facilities, it's huge and offers classes as well (but you have to pay for these). 
The OUSA (Otago University Student Association) has a building which offers so many clubs, really cheap lunches, free weekly breakfasts, they have facilities you can rent for free (a workout room, a sauna), they offer condoms, tampons, pads, safe drug use advice etc. It's a great place to go as a student.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go on weekend trips. You should just get into nature and tramp, hike, drive around and see all the beautiful places NZ has to offer.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Mt. Aoraki was probably the most beautiful national park I've ever seen, close to it is Lake Tekapo and Lake Pukaki. Lake Tekapo is in a dark sky reserve, meaning the stars are stuuuunning.

Fiordland and Milford Sound is a must as well, just stunning. Te Anau is a great hub for going hiking the great walk called the Kepler Track, and where you can stay when visiting Fiordland (if you aren't camping in a tent).

 The Catlins have georgous waterfalls and is only an hour or two south of Dunedin.  
Queenstown is a blast, has partying all year round, adrenaline activities like skydive and bungee jump, and is also a great place for winter sports like skiing and snowboarding. Really fun for a weekend trip w your mates, we did a wine tasting tour of the region. Wanaka is close by Queenstown and is a more chill place for ski sports and beautiful mountain hikes (Roy's Peak fx.) 

Further north is Kaikoura, a little beach town with wonderful water wildlife spotting oppurtunities. You can go whale watching and swimming with dolphins, see a giant seal colony and albatross as well. That place is absolutely glorious and almost spiritual. 
Abel Tasman national park is also really stunning, especially in summer: bays, tropical feel, coastal.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy! My main culture chok when arriving in NZ is that kiwis will greet you with a "how are you?" to which you answer "good, how about you?" before you can start conversation with shop assistants basically. It's nice when you get used to it. Kiwis easily strike up conversations with strangers, which is very foreign to us Danes, but it was actually so nice and freeing to speak to a bunch of people without it being a big deal and just being straight up nice.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I mostly socialized with other exchange students, so can't really help here. But I guess join the clubs, they have so many to choose from!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Probably the extroverted-ness of kiwis is what struck me most. But it was actually really nice to experience.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Kiwis love for and connection to nature. People just go out into nature all the time. And their open-ness to strangers/foreigners, that was so refreshing compared to DK.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. TRAVEL NZ!!!!!!! As much as you can, it is absolutely amazing. Do it with someone, do it alone, just do it! You'll meet amazing people at hostels, at the uni, etc. 
2. Join clubs and attend the O-week, that's a good way to get to know some people and find some friends / get experiences you wouldn't have on your own.
3. Enjoy it.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: (probably shouldn't say this, but the academic level is not as high as at UCPH, at least that wasnt my experience - so dont spend all your time studying haha, just enjoy your time and experiences!)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Learning to travel alone, I felt incredibly independant because now I know I can travel alone, and even move to the other side of the world and meet amazing people and make friends. That's a huge validation for myself about myself, and I'm really proud of it. And obviously, the most reqarding part was seeing beautiful NZ, the mountains are just magical. Everywhere you look is georguos, literally.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Probably missing home, being a bit lonely. And also being stressed about not using my time in NZ to the fullest - which I did, but I felt a little guilty almost sometimes. But that's exactly why I came on exchange, so I could be in NZ for longer and not feel stressed. JS

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: JUST GO TO DUNEDIN, YOU WON'T REGRET IT.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
